bio.en: Logan Kilpatrick is the Head of Developer Relations at OpenAI, supporting developers building on its APIs and ChatGPT, and previously was an ML engineer at Apple.
bio.zh: 洛根·基尔帕特里克（Logan Kilpatrick）是 OpenAI 的开发者关系负责人，支持基于其 API 与 ChatGPT 构建应用的开发者，此前是 Apple 的机器学习工程师。

summary.en: Logan says the top traits he looks for when hiring are high agency and urgency - people who act without needing consensus. He describes being on the front lines as developers figure out how to use AI superpowers in real products. The episode offers a window into OpenAI's developer ecosystem and what makes builders effective in the AI era.
summary.zh: 洛根说，他招聘时最看重的特质是高自驱力与紧迫感——即无需达成共识就能行动的人。他描述了自己身处一线的经历：开发者们正在弄清如何把 AI 的超能力用在真实产品中。本期让我们一窥 OpenAI 的开发者生态，以及在 AI 时代什么让构建者高效。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Finding people who are high agency and work with urgency, if I was hiring five people today, those are some of the top two characteristics that I would look for in people because you can take on the world if you have people who have high agency and not needing to get 50 people's different consensus. They hear something from our customers about a challenge that they're having, and they're already pushing on what the solution for them is and not waiting for all the other things to happen that... People just go and do it and solve the problem, and I love that. It's so fun to be able to be a part of those situations.
turns.zh: 寻找那些自主性强、工作高效的人。如果我今天要招聘五个人，这两个特质绝对是我最看重的。因为如果你能拥有这种自主性强的员工，就无需去征求50个人的不同意见。只要听到客户提到他们面临的挑战，他们就能立即着手寻找解决方案，而不是坐等其他事情先行……员工们会直接行动，解决问题。我特别喜欢这种工作氛围。能参与到这样的场景中，真是太棒了。

turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny. I'm super excited.
turns.zh: 感谢邀请，Lenny。我超级兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to start with the elephant in the room, which I think the elephant is actually leaving the room because I think this is months ago at this point, but I'm still just really curious. What was it like on the inside of OpenAI during the very dramatic weekend with the board and Sam and all those things? What was it like? And is there a story maybe you could share that maybe people haven't heard about what it was like on the inside, what was going on?
turns.zh: 首先，我想先谈谈大家都心知肚明但又避而不谈的事实——OpenAI内部最近发生了诸多动荡。我觉得这头“大象”现在其实已经离开了房间，因为距离事件发生已经过去好几个月了，但我还是很好奇。在OpenAI经历董事会与山姆之间激烈冲突的那个戏剧性周末里，公司内部到底发生了什么？当时的情况究竟如何？有没有什么不为人知的内幕故事可以分享？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, it was definitely a very stressful Thanksgiving week. I think in broad context, OpenAI had been pushing for a really long time, since ChatGPT came out, and that was supposed to be one of the first weeks that the whole company had taken time away to actually reset and have a break. So very selfishly, I was super excited to spend time with my family, all that stuff. And then, yeah, Friday afternoon we got the message that all of the changes were happening, and I think it was super shocking because I think, and this is a perspective a lot of folks share, everybody had and continues to have such deep trust in Sam and Greg and our leadership team that it was just very surprising. And we're also a very, as far as company cultures go, very transparent and very open. So when there's problems or there's things going on, we tend to hear about them. And again, it was the first time that a lot of us had heard some of the things that were happening between the board and the leadership team, so very, very surprising. (00:05:20): I think my being someone who's not based in San Francisco, I was, again, very selfishly kind of happy that it happened over the Thanksgiving break because a lot of folks actually had gone home to different places. So it felt like I had a little bit of comfort knowing I wasn't the only one not in San Francisco, because everybody was meeting up in person to do a bunch of stuff and be together during that time. So it was nice to know that there was a few other folks who were sort of out of the loop with me. (00:05:51): I think the thing that surprised me the most was just how quickly everybody got back to business. I flew to San Francisco the next week after Thanksgiving, which I wasn't planning to do, to deal with the team in person and seeing, literally Monday morning, I was walking into the office being, like expecting, I don't know, something weird to be going on or happening. And really it was like people laser focused and back to work, and I think that speaks to the caliber of our team and everybody who's just so excited about building towards the mission that we're building towards. So I think that was, yeah, that was the most surprising thing of the whole incident. I think a lot of companies would've had the potential to truly be derailed for some non-trivial amount of time by this, and everybody was just right back to it, which I love.
turns.zh:
是的，那确实是一个压力重重的感恩节周。大背景是，自从ChatGPT问世以来，OpenAI就一直在努力推进，而这原本应该是整个公司首次集体休假、调整状态的时机。所以说实话，我特别期待能和家人共度时光，好好放松一下。结果周五下午突然收到消息，得知所有变动即将发生。这真的令人震惊，因为正如许多人所共识的，我们对山姆、格雷格以及管理团队一直充满信任，所以这突如其来的变故着实令人意外。就公司文化而言，我们向来倡导透明开放。所以当内部出现问题或变动时，通常大家都会知情。但这次董事会与管理层之间的矛盾，确实是我们许多人第一次听说，这着实令人惊讶。（00:05:20）  
作为不在旧金山总部的人，我倒是有点庆幸变故发生在感恩节假期期间，因为很多人都回了老家。我知道自己不是唯一一个不在旧金山的人，这让我心里踏实不少。毕竟那段时间大家都忙着开会、聚会，所以能发现还有其他人和我一样被蒙在鼓里，感觉不错。（00:05:51）  
最让我惊讶的是，所有人迅速回归工作的速度之快。感恩节后第二周我就飞回了旧金山，本来没打算去，但还是要亲自与团队沟通。结果周一早上走进办公室时，大家全神贯注地投入工作，完全没有任何异常。这充分说明了我们团队的专业素养，以及每个人对实现使命的热情。我觉得这才是整个事件最令人惊讶的地方。很多公司可能都会被这场风波彻底打乱节奏，但我们团队却迅速回归正轨，这真的令人敬佩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like it also maybe brought the team closer together. It feels like it was this kind of traumatic experience that may bring folks together because it was something they all shared. Is there anything along those lines that's like, "Wow, things are a little different now?"
turns.zh: 我觉得这场风波或许也让团队更加紧密了。这种共同经历的创伤性事件，反而能让大家团结在一起，因为大家都经历了同样的考验。你们有没有类似的感受，比如“哇，现在一切都不一样了”之类的？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: One of my takeaways was I'm actually very grateful that this happened when it happened. I think today the stakes are... They're still relatively high. People have built their businesses on top of OpenAI. We have tons of customers who love ChatGPT, so if something bad happens to us, we definitely impact our customers. But on the world scale, somebody else will build a model if OpenAI disappeared and continue towards this progress of general intelligence. I think fast-forward five or 10 years, if something like this would've happened and we hadn't gone through the hopeful upcoming work transformation and all those changes that are going to happen, I think it would've been a little bit, or potentially much worse, of an outcome. So I'm glad that things happened when the stakes are a little bit lower. (00:07:39): And I totally agree with you. It's like the team has been growing so rapidly over the last year since I joined. It's been crazy to think about how many new folks there are, and I really think that this really brought people together because most folks, historically, many of the folks when I joined, what kind of banded us all together was the launch of ChatGPT, the launch of GPT-4, and for folks who weren't around for some of those launches, it was perhaps step day. For folks who are on for dev day, it was probably this event. So I think we've had these events that have really brought the company together cross-functionally, so hopefully all the future ones will be really exciting things like GPT five, whenever that comes, and stuff like that.
turns.zh: 我的一个感悟是，我其实很庆幸这件事发生在当时那个时间节点。我认为如今的风险……仍然很高。人们在OpenAI之上建立了自己的业务。我们有大量喜爱ChatGPT的客户，所以如果我们遭遇不测，肯定会对客户造成影响。但从全球视角来看，如果OpenAI消失，其他人会继续开发模型，推动通用智能的进程。我觉得五到十年后回头看，如果类似事件发生，而我们没有经历即将到来的工作转型和所有即将发生的变革，结局可能会糟糕得多。所以我很庆幸事情发生在风险相对较低的时候。（00:07:39）：我完全同意你的观点。自从我加入以来，团队在过去一年里发展得非常迅速。回想一下新加入的同事数量，真是令人惊叹。我认为这真的让大家凝聚在了一起，因为大多数人，包括我加入时的大多数人，都是因为ChatGPT和GPT-4的发布而团结在一起的。对于那些没有经历过这些发布的人来说，可能是Step Day。对于参加Dev Day的人来说，可能就是这次活动。所以我认为我们举办的这些活动真的让整个公司在跨职能层面团结起来，希望未来的活动，比如GPT 5的发布之类的，也会同样令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. We're going to talk about GPT-5. Going in a totally different direction, what is the most mind-blowing or surprising thing that you've seen AI do recently?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们要聊聊GPT 5了。说点完全不同的，你最近见过AI做的最令人惊叹或最令人惊讶的事情是什么？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: The things that are getting me most excited are these new interfaces around AI, like the Rabbit R-1. I don't know if you've seen that, but consumer hardware device, this company called TL Draw. I don't know if you've seen TL Draw.
turns.zh: 最让我兴奋的是围绕AI的新界面，比如Rabbit R-1。我不知道你是否见过，但消费级硬件设备，这家叫TL Draw的公司。我不知道你是否见过TL Draw。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think. You sketch something and then it makes it as a website?
turns.zh: 我觉得。你先画个草图，然后它就能把它做成一个网站？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: And that's only a small piece of what TL Draw is actually working on, but there's all of these new interfaces to interact with AI, and I think I was having a conversation with the TL Draw folks a couple of days ago, really blows my mind to think about how chat is the predominant way that folks are using AI today. And I actually think, and this is my bulk case for the folks at TL Draw, I'm super excited for them to build what they're building, but they're sort of building this infinite canvas experience and you can imagine how, as you're interacting with an AI on a daily basis, you might want to jump over to your infinite canvas, which the AI has filled in all the details and you might see a reference to a file and to a video and all of these different things. (00:09:30): And it's such a cool way. It actually makes a lot more sense for us as humans to see stuff in that type of format than, I think, just listing out a bunch of stuff in chat. So I'm really, really excited to see more people. I think 2024 is the year of multimodal AI, but it's also the year that people really push the boundaries of some of these new UX paradigms around AI.
turns.zh: 而这只是TL Draw正在开发的很小一部分内容，但有所有这些与AI交互的新界面。我觉得几天前我和TL Draw的人聊过天，想到如今人们使用AI的主要方式还是聊天，这真的让我很震惊。我实际上认为，对TL Draw的人来说，我对他们正在开发的东西非常兴奋，但他们正在构建这种无限画布体验，你可以想象，当你每天与AI互动时，你可能会想跳到你的无限画布上，AI已经填充了所有细节，你可能会看到一个文件的引用和视频以及所有这些不同的东西。（00:09:30）：这真是很酷的方式。相比于在聊天中列出大量信息，我们人类用这种格式查看东西其实更合理。所以我真的非常期待看到更多人参与进来。我认为2024年是多模态AI之年，但也是人们真正突破围绕AI的一些新用户体验范式的一年。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's funny. I feel like Chatbots, as a PM for many years, it feels like every brainstorming session we had about new features, it's like, "Hey, we should have built a Chatbot to solve this problem." It's like the perennial like, "Oh, Chatbot," or, "Someone's going to suggest we do a Chatbot," and now they're actually useful and working and everyone's building Chatbots, a lot of them based on OpenAI APIs. (00:10:12): There's not really a question there, but maybe the question, I was going to get to this later, is just when people are thinking about building a product like, say, TL Draw, what should they think about? Where OpenAI is not going to go versus here's what OpenAI is going to do for us. We shouldn't worry about them building a version of TL Draw in the future. What's the way to think about where you won't be disrupted essentially by OpenAI, knowing also they may change their mind?
turns.zh: 真有意思。作为一名多年的产品经理，我感觉每次我们开脑暴会讨论新功能时，大家都会说：“嘿，我们应该开发一个聊天机器人来解决这个问题。”就像人们常说的那样，“哦，聊天机器人”，或者“总有人会建议我们做个聊天机器人”。而现在它们确实变得实用且可靠了，大家都在开发聊天机器人，其中很多都基于OpenAI的API。（00:10:12）：这里其实没有具体问题，但我原本想稍后再谈的，是当人们考虑开发产品时，比如TL Draw，他们应该考虑什么？OpenAI不会涉足哪些领域，又会为我们做些什么？我们不必担心他们未来会开发TL Draw的版本。如何避免被OpenAI颠覆，同时又能充分利用他们的技术？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: That's a great question. I think we're deeply focused on these very, very general use cases like the general reasoning capabilities, the general coding, the general writing abilities. I think where you start to get into some of these very vertical applications... And I think a great example of this is actually Harvey. I don't know if you've seen Harvey, but it's this legal AI use case where they're building custom models and tools to help lawyers and people at legal firms and stuff like that. And that's a great example of our models are probably never going to be as capable as some of the things that Harvey's doing because our goal and our mission is really to solve this very general use case and then people can do things like fine-tuning and build all their own custom UI and product features on top of that. (00:11:17): I have a lot of empathy and a lot of excitement for people who are building these very general products today. I talk to a lot of developers who are building just general purpose assistants and general purpose agents and stuff like that. I think it's cool and it's a good idea. I think the challenge for them is they are going to end up directly competing against us in those spaces and I think there's enough room for a lot of people to be successful, but to me you shouldn't be surprised when we end up launching some general purpose agent product because, again, we're sort of building that with GPTs today and versus we're not going to launch some of these varied verticalized products. We're not going to launch an AI sales agent. That's just not what we're building towards. And companies who are and have some domain specific knowledge and they're really excited about that problem space, they can go into that and leverage our models and end up continuing to be on the cutting edge without having to do all that R&D effort themselves.
turns.zh: 这是个很好的问题。我认为我们目前专注于非常通用的应用场景，比如通用推理能力、通用编码、通用写作能力等。当你开始涉及一些垂直应用时，比如Harvey这样的法律AI应用，他们正在构建定制模型和工具来帮助律师和法律事务所等群体。这是一个很好的例子，说明我们的模型可能永远无法像Harvey那样强大，因为我们的目标和使命是解决这些通用应用场景，然后人们可以在此基础上进行微调，构建自己的定制UI和产品功能。（00:11:17）：我对如今开发这些通用产品的团队深表同情和兴奋。我与许多开发通用助手和通用智能体等产品的开发者交流过。我认为这很酷，也是个好主意。但对他们来说，挑战在于他们最终会在这些领域直接与我们竞争。我认为有足够的空间让很多人成功，但对我来说，当我们最终推出通用智能体产品时，你不必感到惊讶，因为我们现在正在用GPTs构建它，而我们不会推出各种垂直产品。我们不会推出AI销售代理。这不是我们的发展方向。那些拥有特定领域知识并对该问题空间充满热情的公司，可以专注于此，利用我们的模型，在无需自己承担大量研发工作的前提下继续保持领先地位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So the advice I'm hearing is get specific about use cases, and that could be either models that are tuned to be especially useful for a use case like sales or make an interface or experience solving a more specific problem.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以我听到的建议是，要明确应用场景，可以是针对销售等场景进行微调的模型，或者打造一个解决更具体问题的界面或体验。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: And I think if you're going to try and solve this very general, if you're going to try to build the next general assistant to compete with something like ChatGPT, it has to be so radically different. People have to really be like, "Wow, this is solving these 10 problems that I have with ChatGPT, and therefore I'm going to go and try your new thing." Otherwise we're just putting a ton of engineering efforts and research effort into making that an incredible product, and it's just going to be the normal challenges of building companies. It's just hard to compete against something like that.
turns.zh: 还有，我认为如果你们要尝试解决这个非常普遍的问题，如果你们要开发一款能与ChatGPT竞争的通用助手，那它必须得有彻底的创新。用户得真心感叹：‘哇，这款产品解决了我对ChatGPT的十大痛点，看来我得去试试你们的新产品了。’否则，我们投入大量工程和研发资源打造出一个出色的产品，最后却只会面临普通企业的挑战。毕竟，要与这样一个巨头竞争实在太难了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, that's great. I was going to get to that later, but I'm glad we touched on that. I imagine that's on the minds of many developers and founders. Kind of along the same lines, there's a lot of talk about how ChatGPT and GPTs and many of the tools you guys offer are going to make a company much more efficient. turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，我正想等下再提到这点，但很高兴我们现在就谈到了。我想这也是许多开发者和创始人关心的问题。类似地，人们常说ChatGPT、GPT以及你们提供的许多工具能让公司变得更高效。不需要那么多工程师、数据科学家、产品经理之类的，但我觉得公司也很难想出切实可行的方法来提高自身效率。我很好奇，你们能否分享一些案例，比如有些公司是如何内部开发GPT工具来解决特定问题，从而节省工程时间，或者是如何利用OpenAI的工具来提升内部业务效率的？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, that's a great question. I wonder if you can put this in the show notes or something like that, but there's a really great Harvard Business School study about... And I forgot which consulting firm they did it with. Maybe it was like Boston Consulting or something like that, but it might've been one of the other ones. And they talk about the order of magnitude of efficiency gain for those folks who are using AI tools, I think it was chat GPT specifically in those use cases that they were using, comparatively against folks who aren't using AI. I'm really excited, also, just as just more time passes between the release of this technology, for us to get more empirical studies. I feel just for myself, as somebody who's an engineer today, I use ChatGPT and I can ship things way faster than I would be able to. (00:14:26): I don't have any good metrics for myself to put a specific number on it, but I'm guessing people are working on those studies right now. I think engineering is actually one of the highest leverage things that you could be using AI to do today and really unlocking, probably on the order of at least a 50% improvement, especially for some of the lower hanging fruit software engineering tasks. The models are just so capable at doing that work. And it's crazy to think... And I'm guessing, actually, GitHub probably has a bunch of really great studies they publish around copilots and you could use those as an analogy for what people are getting from ChatGPT as well. But those are probably the highest leverage things. (00:15:07): I think now with GPTs, people are able to go in and solve some of these more tactical problems. I think one of the general challenges with ChatGPT is it gives a decent answer for a lot of different use cases, but oftentimes it's not particular enough to the voice of your company or the nuance of the work that you're doing. And I think now with GPTs and people who are using the teams in ChatGPT and Enterprise in ChatGPT, they can actually build those things, incorporate the nuance of their own company, and make solving those tasks much, much more domain specific. So we literally just launched GPTs a couple of months ago, so I don't think there's been any good public success stories, but I'm guessing that success is happening right now at companies, and hopefully we'll hear more about that in the months to come as folks get super excited about sharing those case studies.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真是个好问题。我不知道你能否把这个写进节目笔记之类的，但哈佛商学院有一项非常棒的研究……我忘了他们是和哪家咨询公司合作的。可能是波士顿咨询公司之类的，但也可能是其他公司。他们探讨了使用AI工具的人在效率提升方面的量级，我记得具体是在使用ChatGPT的场景中，与不使用AI的人相比效率提升有多大。我也非常期待，随着这项技术发布的时间越来越长，我们能看到更多实证研究。就我个人而言，作为一名工程师，我现在使用ChatGPT，工作效率比以前高得多。我虽然没有具体数据，但我猜现在肯定有人在做相关研究。我认为工程领域是目前使用AI最能提升效率的领域之一，尤其是在一些低门槛的软件工程任务上，效率提升可能达到50%以上。这些模型在处理这类工作时表现得非常出色。真不敢相信……我猜GitHub可能有大量关于Copilot的优秀研究案例，你可以把这些案例类比为人们使用ChatGPT所获得的收益。但这些领域的效率提升潜力确实最大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll share an example. So I have this good friend, his name's Dennis Yang, he works at Chime, and he told me about two things that they're doing at Chime that seem to be providing value. One is he built a GPT that helps write ads for Facebook and Google just gives you ideas for ads to run, and so that takes a little load off the marketing team or the growth team. And then he built another GPT that delivers experiment results, kind of like a data scientist, with here's the result of this experiment. And then you could talk to it and ask for like, "Hey, how much longer do you think we should run this for," or, "What might this imply about our product," and things like that. And I think it's really-
turns.zh: 我举个例子。我有个好朋友叫杨登nis，他在Chime工作。他跟我讲了Chime正在做的两件事，看起来很有价值。第一件是他开发了一个GPT，帮助Facebook和Google写广告，提供投放建议，这样就能减轻营销团队或增长团队的负担。第二件是他开发了另一个GPT，用来提供实验结果，就像数据科学家那样，告诉你实验结果如何。然后你可以和它对话，比如“你觉得这个实验还需要运行多久？”或者“这对我们的产品有什么启示？”之类的。我觉得这真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like you said. Is there anything else that comes to mind? Just things you've heard people do just like, "Wow, that was a really smart way of... " So I get there's engineering, co-piloting type tooling. Is there anything else that comes to mind? Just to give people a little inspiration of like, "Wow, that's an interesting way I should be thinking about using some of these tools."
turns.zh: 正如你所说的。你还能想到其他例子吗？比如你听说过别人做过什么事，比如“哇，这真是个聪明的办法……” 所以我知道有工程类、副驾驶类型的工具。还有其他例子吗？只是想给人们一点启发，让他们想：“哇，这真是个有趣的思路，我应该考虑用这些工具来做些什么。”

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I've seen some interesting GPTs around the planning use cases, like you want to do OKR planning for your team or something like that. I just actually saw somebody tweet it literally yesterday. I've seen some cool venture capital ones of doing diligence on a deal flow, which is kind of interesting, and getting some different perspectives. I think all of those horizontal use cases where you can bring in a different personality and get perspective on different things I think is really cool. I've personally used a GPT, the private GPT that I use myself that helps with some of the planning stuff for different quarters, and just making sure that I'm being consistent in how I'm framing things like driving back to individual metrics, stuff that, when people do planning, they often miss in our data, and then it's been super helpful for me to have a GPT to force me to think about some of those things.
turns.zh: 我见过一些关于规划用例的有趣GPT，比如你想为团队做OKR规划之类的。实际上我昨天刚在推特上看到有人分享。我还见过一些很酷的风险投资案例，比如对交易流进行尽职调查，这挺有意思的，能获得不同的视角。我觉得所有这些横向用例——你能引入不同的思维方式，对不同事物获得不同的视角——都非常酷。我个人用过一个GPT，我自己用的私有GPT，帮助我做不同季度的规划，确保我在构建框架时保持一致性，比如追溯到各个指标之类的。当人们做规划时，他们往往会忽略我们数据中的这些信息，而用GPT来强制思考这些问题，对我来说非常有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, can you talk more about this? What does this GPT do for you and what do you feed it?
turns.zh: 等等，你能多讲讲这个吗？这个GPT能为你做什么？你给它输入了什么？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, I forgot what article I saw online, but it was some article that was talking about what are the best ways to set yourself up for success in planning. And I took a bunch of the... I'll see if I can make it public after this and send you a link, but took a bunch of the examples from that and went in and put some of those suggestions into the GPT, and then now when I do any of my planning of I want to build this thing, I put it through and have it generate a timeline, generate all the specifics of what are the metrics and success that I'm looking for, who might be some important cross-functional stakeholders to include in the planning process, all that stuff, and it's been helpful.
turns.zh: 是的，我忘了在网上看到的是哪篇文章了，但那篇文章讲的是在规划中如何为成功做好准备的最佳方法。我从中选取了许多例子，现在我看看能否公开它，然后给你发个链接，但我把那些例子都输入到了GPT里，现在当我做任何规划，比如我想建这个东西时，我把它放进去，让它生成时间线、生成所有具体的指标和我期望的成功结果、可能需要纳入规划过程的重要跨职能利益相关者之类的，这非常有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is very cool. That would be awesome if you made it public. And if you do, we'll link to it and we'll make it the number one most popular GPT in the store.
turns.zh: 哇，这太酷了。如果你公开它就太棒了。如果你公开了，我们会链接到它，让它成为商店里最受欢迎的GPT。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I love it.
turns.zh: 我喜欢它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Going in a slightly different direction, there's this whole genre of prompt engineering. It feels like it's one of these really emerging skills. I actually saw a startup hiring a prompt engineer, one of the startups I've invested in, and I think that's going to blow a lot of people's minds that there's this new job that's emerging. And I know the idea is this won't last forever, that in theory AI will be so smart you don't need to really think about how to be smart about asking it for things you need it to do. But can you just describe this idea of what is prompt engineering, this term that people might be hearing? And then even more interestingly, just what advice do you have for people to get better at writing prompts for, say, ChatGPT or through the API in general?
turns.zh: 换个方向说，有整个提示工程领域。感觉这是个正在兴起的新技能。我实际上看到一家初创公司在招聘提示工程师，我投资的其中一家初创公司也是这样。我认为很多人会对这种新兴的工作感到惊讶。当然，我知道这不会永远持续下去，理论上AI会变得足够智能，你不需要专门去思考如何巧妙地向它提出你需要它做的事。但你能不能解释一下提示工程这个术语，人们可能听说过这个术语吗？然后更有趣的是，你对人们如何更好地为ChatGPT或一般的API编写提示有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, this is such an interesting space, and I think it's another space where I'm excited for people to do more scientific empirical studies about, because there's so much gut feeling, best practices that maybe aren't actually true in a certain way. I think the reason that prompt engineering exists and comes up at all is because the models are so inclined, because of the way that they're trained, to give you just an answer to the question that you ask. Crap in crap out. If you ask a pretty basic question, you're going to get a pretty basic response. And actually the same thing is true for humans, and you can think of a great example of this. When I go to another human and I ask, "How's your day going," they say, "It's going pretty good." (00:19:53): Literally, absolutely zero detail, no nuance, not very interesting at all versus, again, if you have some context with a person, if you have a personal relationship with them and I ask you, "Hey Lenny, how's your day going? How did the last podcast go," et cetera, et cetera, you just have a little bit more context and agency to go and answer my question. I think this is prompt engineering. (00:20:13): My whole position on this is prompt engineering is a very human thing. When we want to get some value out of a human, we do this prompt engineering. We try to effectively communicate with that human in order to get the best output. And the same thing is true of models. And I think it's like, again, because we're using a system that appears to be really smart, we assume that it has all this context, but it's really like imagine a human level intelligence but literally no context. It has no idea what you're going to ask it. It's never met you before. It has no idea who you are, what you do, what your goals are. And it's the reason that you get super generic responses sometimes is because people forget they need to put that context in the model. (00:20:57): So I think the thing that is going to help solve this problem, and we already kind of do this in the context of Dali, so when you go to the image generation model that we have, Dali, and you say, "I want a picture of a turtle," what it does is it actually takes that description. It says, "I want a picture of a turtle," and it changes it into this high fidelity, like generate a picture of a turtle with a shell, with a green background and lily pads in the water and all this other. It adds all this fidelity because that's the way that the model is trained. It's trained on examples with super high fidelity. This will happen with text models. (00:21:35): You can imagine a world where you go into ChatGPT and you say, "Write me a blog post about AI." It automatically will go and be like, "Let me generate a much higher fidelity description of what this person really wants, which is generate me a blog post about AI that talks about the trade-offs between these different techniques and some example use cases and references some of the latest papers," and it does all that for you, and then you at the user will hopefully be able to be like, "Yep, this is kind of what I wanted. Let me edit this. Let me edit this here." (00:22:02): And again, the inherent problem is we're lazy as humans. We don't want to type all... We don't really want to type what we mean, and I think AI systems are actually going to help solve some of that problem.
turns.zh:
是啊，这个领域实在太有趣了。我认为这又是一个我期待人们能开展更多科学实证研究的领域，因为这里充斥着太多直觉判断和未经验证的"最佳实践"。我觉得提示工程之所以存在且不断涌现，正是因为模型由于训练方式的局限性，总是倾向于直接给出你提问的标准答案——信息量少、缺乏细节、毫无趣味。就拿人类交流来说，你问别人"今天过得怎么样"，他们可能只会回"挺好的"。而如果你和熟人交流，比如"莱尼，最近播客做得怎么样"，他们就能结合上下文更准确地回答。这就是提示工程的本质。

我对此的核心观点是，提示工程本质上是人性化的。当我们想从人类身上获取价值时，就会使用这种提示工程策略。通过有效沟通来获取最佳反馈。模型也是如此。我们总以为它们无所不知，但实际上它们就像缺乏上下文的"人类级智能"——它们不知道你要问什么，从未见过你，不了解你的身份、目标和行为习惯。这就是为什么有时得到的回答过于笼统，因为人们忘记了要在模型中注入这些背景信息。

解决这个问题的关键在于，我们在Dali等平台上已经实践了类似方法。比如，当你使用Dali生成图像模型时，输入"我想要一张乌龟的图片"，模型会将描述转化为超高分辨率图像——带有龟壳的绿色背景、水中睡莲等细节。这是因为模型是在高分辨率样本上训练的。未来文本生成模型也会如此。

可以想象这样的场景：你对ChatGPT说："给我写一篇关于AI的博客文章。"它会自动生成更符合用户需求的描述，比如"让我生成一篇关于AI的博客文章，分析不同技术的权衡，附上案例和最新论文引用"。用户可以直接编辑内容，最终获得理想的结果。

但根本问题在于人类的惰性——我们不愿逐字输入信息，AI或许能帮助我们解决这个难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So until that day, what can people do better when they're prompting, say ChatGPT? And I'll give you an example. Tim Ferris suggested this really good idea that I've been stealing, which is when you're preparing for an interview, you go to chat GPT. And so I did this for you. I was like, "Hey, I'm interviewing Logan Kilpatrick, he is head of developer relations at OpenAI, on my podcast. Give me 10 questions to ask him in the style of Tyler Cowen," who I think is the best interviewer. He is so good at just very pointed original questions. So what advice would you have for me to improve on that prompt to have better results? The questions were fine. They're great. They're interesting enough, but they weren't like, "Holy, these are incredible." So I guess what advice would you give me in that example?
turns.zh: 那么，在那一天到来之前，当人们向ChatGPT提问时，他们能做得更好些什么呢？让我举个例子。蒂姆·费里斯（Tim Ferris）提出了一个非常好的建议，我一直在借鉴。当你准备采访时，可以先去ChatGPT上获取灵感。我为你做了这件事。我当时想：“嘿，我要采访OpenAI的开发者关系主管洛根·基尔帕特里克（Logan Kilpatrick），并在我的播客上播出。给我10个问题，模仿泰勒·考恩（Tyler Cowen）的风格。” 我认为泰勒·考恩是最棒的采访者，他善于提出尖锐且独到的疑问。那么对于如何改进这个提问以获得更好的结果，你们有什么建议吗？这些问题本身不错，很有趣，但并没有让人惊叹到“天哪，这些问题太棒了”的程度。所以在这种情况下，你们会给出什么样的建议呢？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, that's a great example where thinking in context of who it is that you're asking questions about. I'm probably not somebody who has enough information about me on the internet where the model actually has been trained and knows the nuances of my background. I think there's probably much more famous guests where it might be that there's enough context on the internet to answer the questions. You actually have to do some of that work. You need to, say if you're using browse with Bing, for example, you could say, "Here's a link to Logan's blog and some of the things that he's talked about. Here's a link to his Twitter. Go through some of his tweets, go through some of his blogs and see what his interesting perspectives are that we might want to surface on the blog," or something like that. (00:23:36): It's, again, giving the model enough context to answer the question. I think, again, that prompt actually might work really well for somebody who has it, if you were interviewing Tom Cruise or something like that, somebody who has a lot of information about them on the internet. It probably works a little bit better.
turns.zh: 是的，这是一个很好的例子，需要考虑到你要提问的对象是谁。我可能没有足够的网络信息，让模型真正了解我的背景。我认为有些知名嘉宾可能在网上有足够的资料来回答这些问题。在这种情况下，你需要自己做一些功课。比如，如果你使用Bing浏览器，你可以提供链接，指向洛根的博客和他谈论过的内容，以及他的Twitter页面。浏览他的推文和博客，了解他感兴趣的观点，然后在博客中突出这些观点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the advice there is just give more context. It doesn't tell you, "Hey, I don't actually know that much about Logan, so give me some more information." It's just like, "Here you go. Here's a bunch of good questions."
turns.zh: 所以建议就是提供更多背景信息。它不会直接提示：“嘿，我对洛根了解不多，所以给我更多信息。” 而是会说：“给你，这里有一堆好问题。”

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Exactly. It wants to. It so deeply wants to answer your question. It doesn't care that it doesn't have enough context. It's the most eager person in the world you could imagine to answer the question, and without that context it's just hard to do, to give anything a value. If we got t-shirts printed, they should say, "Context is all you need. Context is the only thing that matters." It's such an important piece of getting a language model to do anything for you.
turns.zh: 没错。它非常渴望回答你的问题。它不介意缺乏背景信息。它是世界上最急切回答问题的人，但没有背景信息就很难给出有价值的回答。如果我们印制T恤，应该写上：“背景信息就是你需要的一切。背景信息才是唯一重要的。” 让语言模型为你做任何事情时，背景信息都是至关重要的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Any other tips? Just as people are sitting there, maybe they have ChatGPT open right now as they're crafting a prompt, is there anything else that you'd say would help them have better results?
turns.zh: 还有其他建议吗？当人们坐在那里，可能正在编写提问时，还有什么能帮助他们获得更好的结果呢？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: We actually have a prompt engineering guide, which folks should go and check out. It has some of the examples. It depends on the order of magnitude of how much performance increase you can get. There's a lot of really small silly things, like adding a smiley face, increases the performance of the model. I'm sure folks have seen a lot of these silly examples, but telling the model to take a break and then answer the question, all these kinds of things. And again, if you think about it, it's because the corpus of information that's trained these models is the same things that humans have sent back and forth to each other. So you telling a human, "When I go take a break and then I come back to work, I'm fresher and I'm able to answer questions better and do work better," so very similar things are true for these models. And again, when I see a smiley face at the end of someone's message, I feel empowered that this is going to be a positive interaction and I should be more inclined to give them a great answer and spend more effort on the thing that they asked me for.
turns.zh: 实际上我们有一份提示工程指南，大家可以去看看。里面有一些示例。这取决于你能获得多大程度的性能提升。有些很小的细节，比如添加一个笑脸，就能提升模型的性能。我相信大家见过很多这类例子，比如告诉模型休息一下再回答问题之类的。再想一想，这是因为训练这些模型的语料库，正是人类之间反复交流的内容。所以你对人类说"我休息一下再回来工作，会更清醒，能更好地回答问题"，这对模型来说也是类似的道理。还有，当我在别人消息末尾看到笑脸时，会觉得这会是一次积极的互动，我应该更愿意给出优质的回答，投入更多精力处理他们的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, wait. So that's a real thing. If you had a smiley face, it might give you better results.
turns.zh: 哇，等等。所以这确实是真的。如果你加个笑脸，可能会得到更好的结果。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Again, it's like the challenge with all this stuff is it's very nuanced and it's also it's a small jump in performance. You could imagine on the order of one or 2%, which for a few sentence answer might not even be a discernible difference. Again, if you're generating an entire saga of texts, the smiley face could actually make a material difference for you, but for something small and textual it might not.
turns.zh: 再说一次，所有这些东西的挑战在于它非常微妙，而且性能提升幅度也很小。你可以想象，提升1%或2%，对几句话的回答来说可能根本察觉不到差异。当然，如果你要生成一整段文本，笑脸可能会对性能产生实质性影响，但对于简短的文本可能效果不明显。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, good tip. Amazing. Okay, we've talked about GPTs I think maybe might be helpful to describe what is this new thing that you guys launched, GPTs, and I'm curious just how it's going. This is a really big change and element of OpenAI now with this idea that you could build your own mini, and I'm almost explaining it, your mini open ChatGPT and then people can... I think you can pay for it. You can charge for your own GPT or is it all free right now?
turns.zh: 好的，不错。太棒了。好的，我们已经讨论了GPT，我想也许可以讲讲你们推出的新东西GPT，我很好奇进展如何。这对OpenAI来说是个重大变化，现在有了可以自己搭建迷你ChatGPT的想法，我几乎要解释一下了，就是你可以搭建自己的迷你ChatGPT，然后人们可以……我觉得可以收费吧。你可以收费使用自己的GPT，还是现在都是免费的？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: It's ll free right now. It's all free.
turns.zh: 现在都是免费的。完全免费。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. In the future I imagine people will be able to charge. So there's this whole store now. Basically it's the whole app store that you guys have launched. How's it going? What's happening? What surprised you there? What should people know?
turns.zh: 好的。我猜未来人们应该可以收费了。现在有整个商店了。基本上就是你们推出的整个应用商店。进展如何？有什么惊喜吗？大家需要知道些什么？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, it's going great, and again, historically the thing that you would have to do, let's say for example, you have a really cool ChatGPT use case, what you would have to do to share it with somebody else is actually go in and start the conversation with the model, prompt it to do the things that you wanted to, and then you would share that link with somebody else before the action has actually happened and be like, here now you can essentially finish this conversation with ChatGPT that I started. (00:27:08): So GPT kind of changes this where you take all that important context, you put it into the model to begin with, and then people can go and chat with essentially a custom version of ChatGPT. And the thing that's really interesting is you can upload files, you can give it custom instructions, you can add all these different tools. Like a code interpreter is built in, which allows you to do math. Essentially you have browsing built in, image generation built in. You can also, for more advanced use cases if you're a developer, you can connect it to external APIs so you can connect it to the Notion API or Gmail or all these different things, and have it actually take actions on your behalf. (00:27:44): So there's so many cool things that people are unlocking. And what's been most exciting to me, actually, is the non-developer persona is now empowered to go and solve these really, really, really more challenging problems by giving the model enough context on what that problem is to be able to solve it. Going back to context is all you need, this is very true in the context of GPTs, and if you give it enough context, you can solve much more interesting problems. (00:28:11): There's so many things that I'm excited about with this. I think monetization, when it comes to the store later this quarter, I think is going to be extremely exciting when people can get paid based on who's using their GPT. That's going to be a huge unlock and open a lot of people's eyes to the opportunity here. I also think continuing to push on making more capabilities accessible to GPTs for people who can't code is really exciting. Even for me as someone who is a software engineer, it's not super easy to connect the Notion API or the Gmail API to my GPT, and really I'd love to just be able to one click sign in with Gmail and then all of a sudden it's like my Gmail is accessible, or someone else can sign in with their Gmail and make it accessible. So I think over time all those types of things will come, but today it's really custom prompts is essentially one of the biggest value adds with GPTs.
turns.zh: 是的，进展非常顺利。再说回来，从历史上看，要想与他人分享一个很棒的ChatGPT应用案例，你得先启动与模型的对话，提示它完成你想要的任务，然后在实际操作完成前把链接分享给别人，再让对方接手继续与ChatGPT对话。（00:27:08）但GPT改变了这一流程——你可以把所有关键信息提前输入模型，然后用户就能直接使用定制版的ChatGPT进行交流。最有趣的是，它支持上传文件、自定义指令，还能集成代码解释器、图像生成器等工具。更高级的应用场景下，开发者可以接入外部API，比如Notion API、Gmail等，实现自动化操作。（00:27:44）人们正在解锁诸多新功能。最让我兴奋的是，非技术用户现在也能通过为模型提供充足上下文来解决极具挑战性的问题。归根结底，关键在于上下文——这在GPT技术中至关重要。只要提供足够的背景信息，就能解决更多复杂难题。（00:28:11）我对这项技术充满期待。今年第三季度即将上线商店功能，届时用户能基于GPT的使用获得收益，这将释放巨大价值，吸引更多人关注其中的商机。持续为非编程用户赋能，让他们能更便捷地接入GPT功能同样令人振奋。就连我这样的软件工程师，要想把Notion API或Gmail API接入自己的GPT也并非易事——我特别希望能一键登录Gmail，让别人也能轻松访问我的邮箱数据。相信未来这些功能会逐步实现，但当下自定义提示仍是GPT最核心的价值所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I have it pulled up here on different monitor and Canva has the top GPT currently, and I was trying to play with it as you're chatting just to see. I was going to make a big banner that said, "It's the context stupid," and it doesn't. I'm not doing something right, but I'm not paying that much attention to it because we're talking, but this is very cool. Just maybe a final question there. Is there a GPT that you saw someone built that was like, "Wow, that's amazing. That's so cool," something that surprised you? And I'll share one that was very cool, but is there anything that comes to mind when I ask that?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我现在在另一台显示器上打开了Canva，目前它是顶流的GPT。我正尝试模仿你的对话过程看看效果。本来想做个大横幅写“关键在于上下文，笨蛋”，但没成功。可能是我操作有误，不过我们聊得太投入，也没太注意细节。不过这确实很酷。最后再问个问题，有没有看到别人开发的特别惊艳的GPT案例？我分享一个特别酷的，但你有没有类似的灵感？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I think my instinct is the Zapier. All of the stuff that Zapier has done with GPTs is the most useful stuff that you could imagine. You can go so far with what... And I don't know how it's packaged for Zapier's GPT right now, but you can actually, as a third party developer, integrate Zapier without knowing how to code into your GPT. So they're pushing a lot of this stuff, and then basically all 5,000 connections that are possible with Zapier today, you can bring into your GPT and essentially enable it to do anything. So I'm incredibly excited for Zapier and for people who are building with them so many things that you can unlock using that platform. So I think that's probably the most exciting thing to me for people who aren't developers.
turns.zh: 我觉得我的直觉告诉我应该选Zapier。Zapier在GPT方面所做的一切都是你能想象到的最实用的东西。用Zapier，你可以做得非常深入……我不知道Zapier目前的GPT接口是如何打包的，但作为第三方开发者，你实际上可以无需编程知识就将Zapier集成到你的GPT中。他们正在大力推广这些功能，而且目前Zapier支持的5000种连接方式，你都可以引入到你的GPT中，从而让它具备几乎无限的功能。我对Zapier以及那些利用它平台开发各种应用的人感到无比兴奋。所以对我来说，对于非开发者来说，这可能是最激动人心的事情了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Zapier's always in there, getting in there connecting things.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Zapier总是能把各种东西连接起来。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, they're great.
turns.zh: 是啊，他们真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the one that I had in mind, so I had a buddy of mine, [inaudible 00:30:28], who's the CEO of a company called Runway built this thing called Universal Primer which helps you learn. It's described as, "Learn everything about anything," and basically, I think, it's kind of this Socratic method of helping you learn stuff. So it's like, "Explain how transformers work in LMs," and then it just kind goes through stuff and then asks you questions, I think, and helps you learn new concepts. And I think it's the number two education GPT.
turns.zh: 我之前想到了一个例子，我有个朋友[音频不清00:30:28]，他是一家叫Runway的公司的CEO，开发了一个叫Universal Primer的工具，帮助你学习。它的宣传语是“了解任何事情的方方面面”，基本上，我觉得它采用的是苏格拉底式的教学方法，帮助你学习知识。比如，它会问你“解释Transformer在语言模型中的工作原理”，然后带着你逐步理解，接着再提问，帮助你掌握新概念。我觉得它是教育领域第二受欢迎的GPT。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I love that. [inaudible 00:30:53] is incredible, so...

Creating a product demo has never been easier. With browser-based recording Arcade is the no-code solution for building personalized demos at scale. Ready to tell more engaging product stories that drive results? Head to arcade.software/lenny and get 50% off your first three months. That's arcade.software/lenny. (00:32:11): I want to talk about just what it's like to work at OpenAI and how the product team operates and how the company operates. So you worked at... Your two previous companies were Apple and NASA, which are not known for moving fast. And now you're at OpenAI, which is known for moving very fast, maybe too fast for some people's taste, as we saw it with the whole board thing. And so what I'm curious is just what is it that OpenAI does so well that allows them to build and ship so quickly and at such a high bar? Is there a process or a way of working that you've seen that you think other companies should try to move more quickly and ship better stuff?
turns.zh: 是的，确实如此。让我跟你介绍一款叫做Arcade的产品。Arcade是一个互动演示平台，能让团队在几分钟内创建精良且符合品牌形象的演示文稿。向客户讲述产品故事并非易事，他们更希望你展示产品本身，而非仅止于口头描述或设置访问门槛。这就是为什么Atlassian、Carta和Retool等产品团队会借助Arcade，在主页、产品变更日志、邮件和文档中更好地传递产品价值。（00:31:23）但别只听我一面之词。领先的数字分析平台Quantum Metric就曾创建互动产品演示库，以此吸引更多潜在客户。借助Arcade，他们的演示转化率提升了两倍，用户参与度更是视频的五倍。此外，产品演示的制作速度比以往快了十倍。创建产品演示从未如此简单。基于浏览器的录制功能，使Arcade成为大规模构建个性化演示的无代码解决方案。（00:31:50）Arcade提供产品定制选项、设计师认可的编辑工具，并全程追踪用户行为数据。准备好讲述更引人入胜、能推动业务成果的产品故事了吗？访问arcade.software/lenny，即可享受首三个月50%折扣优惠。（00:32:11）我想聊聊在OpenAI工作的感受，探讨产品团队的运作模式及公司整体运营方式。您之前曾在苹果和NASA工作，这两家公司以行动迟缓著称。而如今您在OpenAI任职，众所周知该公司行动速度极快——正如董事会事件所暴露的，有些人甚至认为速度过快。您能否分享OpenAI的成功秘诀？是某种流程或工作方式让他们能以如此高的标准快速开发并发布产品？您是否发现了其他公司可以借鉴的加速创新、提升交付质量的实践？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, there's so many interesting trade-offs and all of this tension around how quickly companies can move. I think for us, again, if you think about Apple as an example, if you think about NASA as an example, just older institutions, lots of... Over time, the tendency is things slow down. There's additional checks and balances that are put in place, which drags things down a little bit. So we're young and a new company, so we don't have a lot of that institutional legacy barriers that have been put in place. (00:33:18): I think the biggest thing, and there's a good Sam tweet somewhere in the ether about this from, I think, 2022 or something like that, but finding people who are high agency and work with urgency is one of the most... If I was hiring five people today, those are some of the top two characteristics that I would look for in people because you can take on the world if you have people who have high agency and not needing to either get 50 people's different consensus, because you have people who you trust with high agency and they can just go and do the thing, I think, is one of the most... It is the most important thing, I'm pretty sure, if you were to distill it down. (00:34:04): And I see this in folks that I work with. Folks are so high agency. They see a problem and they go and tackle it. They hear something from our customers about a challenge that they're having and they're already pushing on what the solution for them is and not waiting for all the other things to happen that I think traditional companies are stuck behind because they're like, "Oh, let's check with all these seven different departments to try to get feedback on this." People just go and do it and solve the problem. And I love that. It's so fun to be able to be a part of those situations.
turns.zh: 是啊，有很多有趣的权衡取舍，以及围绕公司运作速度的种种矛盾。我觉得对我们而言，再以苹果为例，再以NASA为例，这些老牌机构往往……随着时间推移，事物往往会变得迟缓。会有更多的制衡机制被建立起来，这会拖慢进程。所以我们是一家年轻的新公司，没有那些根深蒂固的制度障碍。（00:33:18）：我认为最重要的一点——我记得2022年左右Sam在推特上提过这件事——就是找到那些积极主动、行动高效的人才。这是我现在招聘时最看重的两个特质，因为只要有高度积极主动的人才，你就能征服世界。他们无需征求50人的共识，因为你信任他们，他们能直接行动。我认为这才是最重要的——如果你要总结的话，这绝对是核心要素。（00:34:04）：我在同事身上也看到了这种特质。他们行动力超强。一旦发现问题，就立刻着手解决。一旦听说客户遇到挑战，就立即思考解决方案，而不必等待其他部门的反馈——传统公司可能因为这种拖拉而停滞不前。人们只管行动，解决问题。这种工作氛围太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so cool. I really like these two characteristics because I haven't heard this before. Those are the two, maybe the two most important things you guys look for, high agency, high urgency. To give people a clear sense of what these actually look like when you're hiring, you shared maybe this example of customer service. Someone's hearing a bug and then going to fix it. Is there anything else that can illustrate what that looks like, high agency? And then a similar question on urgency other than just move, move, move, ship, ship, ship.
turns.zh: 这太酷了。我真的很喜欢这两个特质，因为我以前从未听过相关讨论。积极主动和行动高效，或许是你们最看重的两个特质。能否举个招聘实例，让大家更直观理解这两个特质？比如客户服务部门遇到问题后，有人能立即着手修复。这类例子还有吗？除了“行动、行动、行动”和“快速交付”之外，是否还有其他能说明行动力强、紧迫感强的例子？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I think the assistants API that we released for dev day, we continue to get this feedback from developers that people wanted these higher levels of abstraction on top of our existing APIs, and a bunch of folks on the team just came together and were like, "Hey, let's put together what the plan would look like to build something like this," And then very quickly came together and actually built the actual API that now powers so many people's assistant applications that are out there. And I think that's a great example of it wasn't this top down, oh, someone's sitting there being like, "Oh, let's do these five things," and then like, "Okay, team, go and do that." It's like people really seeing these problems that are coming up and knowing that they can come together as a team and solve these problems really quickly. And I think the assistants API, and there's like 1,001 other examples of teams taking agency and doing this, but I think that's a great one at the top of my head
turns.zh: 我觉得我们在开发者日发布的助手API，就很好地说明了这一点。开发者反馈说，他们希望在现有API基础上获得更高层次的抽象。团队成员迅速行动起来，共同规划如何构建这样的系统。最终，我们很快就开发出了这个API，现在它为众多助手应用提供支持。我认为这是一个很好的例子，说明这不是自上而下的决策过程——不是某个人坐在那里说：“我们要做这五件事”，然后再命令团队去执行。而是团队成员主动发现问题，知道如何迅速团结起来解决问题。我觉得助手API就是一个很好的例子，还有无数其他团队通过积极主动、快速行动的例子，但这确实是我能随口想到的最典型案例之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes me want to ask. Just how does planning work at OpenAI? So in this example is just like, "Hey, we think we need to build this. Let's just go and build it." I imagine there's still a roadmap and priorities and goals and things that that team had. How does road mapping and prioritization and all of that generally work to allow for something like that?
turns.zh: 这让我不禁想问，OpenAI 的规划流程到底是怎样的？以这个例子来说，他们可能就是这样做的："嘿，我们觉得需要开发这个功能，那就直接动手开发吧。"我相信团队肯定有路线图、优先级排序、目标设定等流程，但具体如何运作才能实现这样的成果呢？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I think this is one of the more challenging pieces at OpenAI. There's so many. Everyone wants everything from us, and today, especially, in the world of ChatGPT and how large and well-used our API is, people will just come to us and say, "Hey, we want all of these things." I think there's a bunch of core guiding principles that we look at. One, going back to the mission, is this actually going to help us get to AGI? So there's a huge focus on there's this potential shiny reward right in front of us, which is optimize user engagement, or whatever it is. And is that really the thing? Maybe the answer is yes. Maybe that is what is going to help us get to AGI sooner, but looking at it through that lens I think is always the first step of deciding any of these problems. (00:37:03): I think, on the developer side, there's also these core tenets of reliability like, "Hey, it would be awesome if we had additional APIs that did all these cool things like new endpoints, new modalities, new abstractions, but are we giving customers a robust and reliable experience on our API?" And that's often the first question. And I think there have been times where we've fallen short on that, and there was a bunch of other things that we've been thinking about doing and really bringing the focus and priority back to that reliability piece because, at the end of the day, nobody cares if you have something great if they can't use it robust and reliably. (00:37:37): So there's these core tenets. And I think, again, we have very, other than all the principles about how we're making the decision, I think the actual planning process is pretty standard. We come together. There's H1 Q1 goals. We all sprint on those. I think the real interesting thing is how stuff changes over time. You think we're going to do these very high level things and new models, new modalities, whatever it is. And then as time goes on, there's all of this turmoil and change, and it's interesting to have mechanisms to be like, "Hey, how do we update our understanding of the world and our goals as everything the ground changes underneath of us as is happening in the craziness of the AI space today?"
turns.zh: 我认为这正是 OpenAI 面临的最具挑战性的问题之一。我们面临着各种各样的需求，每个人都希望从我们这里获得一切。尤其是在 ChatGPT 时代，以及我们的 API 如此普及的情况下，人们会直接来找我们说："嘿，我们需要这些功能。"我们需要遵循一系列核心指导原则。首先，回归到使命本身——这真的能帮助我们实现通用人工智能（AGI）吗？因此，我们高度关注眼前看似诱人的奖励，比如优化用户参与度之类的。但这真的是关键所在吗？或许答案是肯定的。或许这能帮助我们更快地实现 AGI，但从这个角度出发，始终是解决任何问题的第一步。（00:37:03）：在开发者层面，还有一些可靠性的核心原则，比如："如果我们能增加新的 API，支持新端点、新模态、新的抽象概念，那当然很棒，但我们是否能为客户提供稳定可靠的 API 体验呢？"这往往是首要考量。我们曾在这方面有所欠缺，也有过其他想做却未能实现的计划，最终将重点和优先级重新放回可靠性层面，因为归根结底，如果产品无法稳定可靠地使用，再好的功能也没意义。（00:37:37）：这些核心原则至关重要。除了这些决策准则，实际的规划流程其实相当标准。我们会共同制定目标，分阶段推进。但真正有趣的是，随着时间推移，事情总会发生变化。当我们计划实现高层次的功能，如新模型、新模态等时，随着 AI 领域的疯狂变革，底层环境不断变化，我们如何更新对世界的理解和目标呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting that it sounds a lot like most other companies. There's H1 planning. There's Q1 planning. Are there metrics and goals like that that you guys have OKRs or anything like that? Or is it just, Here we're going to launch these products?"
turns.zh: 有趣的是，这听起来和大多数其他公司很像。你们有季度规划吗？有没有 OKRs 之类的目标管理系统？还是只是直接说‘我们要发布这些产品’？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I think it's much higher level. I actually don't think OpenAI is a big OKR company. I don't think teams do OKRs today and I don't have a good understanding of why that's the case, whether or not. I don't even know if OKRs are still the industry. You're probably talking to a lot more folks about who are making those decisions. So I'm curious. Is that something that you're seeing from folks? Is it still common for people to do OKRs?
turns.zh: 我认为 OpenAI 的规划层级更高。我不认为 OpenAI 是一家大规模使用 OKRs 的公司。如今团队似乎不怎么用 OKRs 了，我也不太清楚为什么会这样，甚至不知道 OKRs 是否还在业界流行。你可能需要去问更多负责决策的人。所以我很好奇，你们有没有遇到过使用 OKRs 的人？现在人们还普遍使用 OKRs 吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Many companies use OKRs, love OKRs. Many companies hate OKRs. I'm not surprised that OpenAI is not an OKR driven company. Along those lines, I don't know how much you can share about all this stuff, but how do you measure success for things that you launch? I know there's this ultimate goal, AGI. Is there some way to track we're getting closer? What else do you guys look at when you launch, say DPT Store or assistants or anything that's like, "Cool, that was exactly what we're hoping for." Is it just adoption?
turns.zh: 是的，绝对正确。许多公司使用OKR，热爱OKR。也有许多公司讨厌OKR。我一点也不惊讶OpenAI不是一家以OKR为驱动的公司。说到这，我不知道你能透露多少信息，但对于你们推出的产品，你们如何衡量其成功与否？我知道最终目标是通用人工智能（AGI）。有没有什么方法能追踪我们正在接近这个目标的进展？当你们推出新产品时，比如DPT Store、智能助手之类的，有没有什么让人惊喜的时刻，觉得“哇，这正是我们期望的结果”？仅仅是用户接受度吗？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, adoption is a great one. I think there's a bunch of metrics around revenue, number of developers that are building on our platform, all those things. And a lot of these, and I don't want to dive... I'll let Sam or someone else on our leadership team go more into details, but I think a lot of these are actual abstractions towards something else. Even if revenue is a goal, it's like revenue is not actually the goal. Revenue is a proxy for getting more compute, which is then actually what helps us get towards getting more GPUs so that we can train better models and actually get to the goal. So there's all these intermediate layers where even if we say something is the goal, and you hear that in a vacuum and you're like, "Oh, well OpenAI just wants to make money," and it's like, "Well, really money is the mechanism to get better models so that we can achieve our mission." And I think there's a bunch of interesting angles like that as well.
turns.zh: 是的，用户接受度是个很重要的指标。我认为衡量标准包括收入、在我们平台上开发的开发者数量等等。很多指标——我不想深入探讨细节——但我认为很多指标其实是通向其他目标的抽象指标。即使收入是目标，但它本身并非最终目标。收入是获取更多计算资源的指标，而计算资源反过来又能帮助我们获得更多GPU，从而训练出更优质的模型，最终实现目标。因此，存在诸多中间环节。即便我们把某个指标称为目标，如果你孤立地看待它，就会觉得“哦，OpenAI就是想赚钱”，其实不然。赚钱只是获取更优质模型的手段，最终才能实现我们的使命。这类有趣的思路还有很多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if I've heard of a more ambitious vision for a company, to build artificial general intelligence. I love that. I imagine many companies are like, "What's our version of that?" Before we leave this topic, is there anything else that you've seen OpenAI do really well that allows it to move this fast and be this successful? You talked about hiring people with higher agency and high urgency. Is there anything else that's just like, "Oh wow, that's a really good way of operating?" I imagine part of it's just hiring incredibly smart people. I think that's probably an unsaid thing, but yeah, anything else?
turns.zh: 我从未听说过有哪家公司有比OpenAI更宏伟的愿景——构建通用人工智能。我很欣赏这一点。相信很多公司都在思考：“我们的版本会是什么样？”在结束这个话题之前，你是否注意到OpenAI在哪些方面做得特别出色，助力其发展如此迅速、如此成功？你提到招聘高代理能力和高紧迫感的人才。还有其他值得借鉴的方面吗？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I think there's a non-trivial benefit to using Slack, and I think maybe that's controversial and maybe some people don't like Slack, but OpenAI has such a slack heavy culture and it really... The instantaneous real time communication on Slack is so crucial. And I just love being able to tag in different people from different teams and get everybody coalesced. So everybody is always on Slack, so even if you're remote or you're on a different team or in a different office, so much of the company culture is ingrained in Slack, and it allows us to really quickly coordinate where it's actually faster to send someone a Slack message sometimes than it would be to walk over to their desk because they're on Slack and they're going to be using it. (00:41:27): And I saw, if you saw, the recent Sam and Bill Gates interview, but Sam was talking about how Slack is his number one most used app on his phone and, "I don't even look at the time thing on my phone anymore because I don't want to know how long I'm using Slack," but I'm sure the Salesforce people are looking at the numbers and they're like, "This is exactly what we wanted."
turns.zh: 我认为使用Slack确实带来了显著的好处。这或许有些争议，可能有些人不喜欢Slack，但OpenAI的Slack文化根深蒂固。Slack上即时实时的沟通至关重要。我喜欢能在不同团队中@不同成员，快速汇聚各方力量。所有人都时刻在线，远程工作者或不同团队、不同办公室的成员也能顺畅协作。Slack已经深度融入公司文化，有时发送Slack消息比走过去办公室更高效。（00:41:27）我看到最近萨姆和比尔·盖茨的采访，萨姆称Slack是他手机上使用最多的应用，“我甚至不再看手机时间，因为不想知道自己用了多久Slack”。但我相信Salesforce团队肯定在关注数据，他们会感叹：“这正是我们想要的结果。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also love Slack. I'm a big promoter Slack. I think there's a lot of Slack hate, but such a good product. I've tried so many alternatives and nothing compares. I think what's interesting about Slack for you guys is one of the... You don't know if someone in there is just an AGI, that is not actually a person that's just there working at the company.
turns.zh: 我也超爱Slack。我是Slack的忠实拥趸。我觉得人们对Slack有很多负面评价，但它确实是个很棒的产品。我试过很多替代品，但都比不上它。我觉得Slack对你们来说有趣的地方在于，里面的人有些可能是AGI（通用人工智能），而不是真正在公司工作的真人。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: I know there are real people. There is no AGIs yet. But I think, yeah, even Slack is building a bunch of really cool AI tools, which I'm excited to... And that's why there's so much cool AI progress. And at the end of the day, it's so exciting, from being a consumer of all these new AI products. Google's a great example. I'm so happy that Google is doing really cool AI stuff because I'm a Google Docs customer and I love using Google Docs. I like a bunch of their other products, and it's awesome that people are building such useful things around these models.
turns.zh: 我知道确实有真人用户。目前还没出现AGI。但我觉得，即便Slack也在开发一堆超酷的人工智能工具，我对此也特别兴奋……这就是为什么人工智能领域有这么多酷炫的进展。说到底，作为这些新人工智能产品的消费者，真的太激动了。谷歌就是个很好的例子。我很高兴谷歌在做超酷的人工智能项目，因为我是谷歌文档的用户，我超爱用谷歌文档。我还喜欢他们的其他很多产品，能看到人们围绕这些模型开发出这么实用的东西，真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How big is the OpenAI team at this point, whatever you can share? Just to give people a sense of the scale.
turns.zh: OpenAI团队目前规模有多大？能透露一些信息吗？让大家对其规模有个概念。

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, I think the last public number was something around like 750 near the end of last year, 780 or something like that near the end of last year. And we're still growing so quickly, so I won't be the messenger to share the specific updated numbers, but the team is growing like crazy and we're also hiring across all of our engineering teams and PM teams, so folks who are interested, would love to hear from folks who are curious about joining.
turns.zh: 是的，我记得去年年底公开的数字是750人左右，或者780人左右。我们的团队增长速度非常快，所以我不方便透露具体的最新数字，但团队规模正在疯狂扩张，我们所有的工程团队和产品经理团队都在招人，有兴趣的人可以联系我们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe one last question here. So you're growing, maybe getting to 1,000 people, clearly still very innovative and moving incredibly fast. Is there anything you've seen about what OpenAI does well to enable innovation and not slow down new big ideas?
turns.zh: 最后再问一个问题。你们团队在不断壮大，可能快到1000人了，显然依然非常有创新力，发展速度惊人。有没有什么好的做法能让OpenAI保持创新不拖慢新想法的进度？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, there's a couple of things, one of which is the actual research team, who seed most of the innovation that happens at OpenAI, is intentionally small. Most of the growth that OpenAI has seen is around our customer facing roles, our engineering roles to provide the infrastructure for ChatGPT and things like that. The research team is, again, intentionally kept small and there's all of this talk. And it's really interesting. I just saw this thread from one of our research folks who was talking about how in a world where you're constrained by the amount of GPU capacity that you have as a researcher, which is the case for open AI researchers, but also researchers everywhere else, each new researcher that you add is actually a net productivity loss for the research group unless that person is up-leveling everyone else in such a profound way that it increases the efficiency. (00:44:12): If you just add somebody who's going to go and tackle some completely different research direction, you now have to share your GPUs with that person and everyone else is now slower on their experiments. So it's a really interesting trade-off that research folks have that I don't think product folks... If I add another engineer to our API team or to some of the ChatGPT teams, you can actually write more code and do more. And that's actually a net beneficial improvement for everybody. And that's always not the case in the case of researchers, which is interesting, in A GPU constrained world, which hopefully we won't always be in.
turns.zh: 有几个方面。首先，负责大部分创新研发的研究团队故意保持小规模。OpenAI的大部分增长来自面向客户的角色，比如提供ChatGPT基础设施的工程团队。研究团队故意保持小规模，关于这个话题有很多讨论。这真的很有趣。我刚看到我们研究团队的一个成员发的帖子，讲的是在一个GPU资源受限的世界里（比如OpenAI的研究者，以及其他所有研究者），每增加一个新研究者实际上都会降低整个团队的生产力效率，除非这个新人能以某种深刻的方式提升其他人的效率。（00:44:12）如果你只是增加一个去探索完全不同研究方向的人，你就得和他共享GPU资源，导致其他人的实验速度变慢。这对研究者来说是个很微妙的权衡，我觉得产品团队不会遇到这种情况。如果我给API团队或ChatGPT团队再增加一个工程师，他们就能写更多代码，做更多事情。这对大家来说确实是净收益。而研究者的情况并非如此，这挺有趣的，尤其是在GPU受限的世界里，但希望我们不会一直处于这种状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to zoom out a bit and then there's going to be a couple follow-up questions here. Where are things heading with OpenAI? What's in the near future of what people should expect from the tools that you guys are going to have in launch?
turns.zh: 我想先把视野拉宽一点，然后再回答几个后续问题。OpenAI的发展方向如何？未来人们对即将推出的工具能有怎样的期待？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, new modalities. I think ChatGPT continuing to push all of the different experiences that are going to be possible. Today, ChatGPT is really just text in, text out or, I guess three months ago, it was just text in, text out. We started to change that with now you can do the voice mode and now you can generate images and now you can take pictures. So I think continuing to expand the way in which you interface with AI through ChatGPT is coming. (00:45:24): I think GPTs is our first step towards the agent future. Again, today when you use A GPT, it's really you send a message, you get an answer back almost right away, and that's kind of the end of your interaction. I think as GPTs continue to get more robust, you'll actually be able to say, "Hey, go and do this thing and just let me know when you're done. I don't need the answer right now. I want you to really spend time and be thoughtful about this." (00:45:48): And again, if you think back to all these human analogies, that's what we do as humans. I don't expect somebody, when I ask them to do something meaningful for me, to do it right away and give me the answer back right away. So I think pushing more towards those experiences is what is going to unlock so much more value for people. (00:46:06): And I think the last thing is GPTs as this mechanism to get the next few hundred million people into ChatGPT and into AI. So I think if you've had conversations with people who aren't close to the AI space, oftentimes you talk about, even if they've heard of ChatGPT... A lot of people haven't heard of ChatGPT, but if they have, they show up in ChatGPT and they're like, "I don't really know what I'm supposed to do with this blank slate. I can kind of do anything. It's not super clear how this solves my specific problem." (00:46:35): But I think the cool thing about GPTs is you can package down like, "Here's this one very specific problem that AI can solve for you and do it really well," and I can share that experience with you and now you can go and try that GPT, have it actually solve the problem and be like, "Wow, it did this thing for me. I should probably spend the time to investigate these five other problems that I have to see if AI can also be a solution to those." So I think so many more people are going to come online and start using these tools because very narrow vertical tools are what's going to be a huge unlock for them.
turns.zh: 是的，新的模态。我认为ChatGPT会继续推动各种可能的体验。如今，ChatGPT还是单纯的文本输入与输出——三个月前甚至只有文本输入与输出。现在我们增加了语音模式、图像生成和拍照功能。所以我觉得通过ChatGPT与AI交互的方式将不断拓展。（00:45:24）：我认为GPT是我们迈向智能体未来的第一步。如今使用GPT时，用户发送消息后几乎立即得到回复，互动就此结束。但随着GPT功能日益强大，用户将能真正对它说：“去完成这项任务，完成后再通知我。我现在不需要即时答案，我希望你能花时间深思熟虑。”（00:45:48）：再回想人类行为的类比，我们也会这样做。当我请求他人为我做有意义的事时，绝不会期望他们立刻回复。所以推动这种交互体验的进化，将为人们释放更多价值。（00:46:06）：最后一点是，GPT将成为吸引数亿人使用ChatGPT和AI的机制。与不熟悉AI领域的人交谈时，你会发现即便他们听说过ChatGPT……许多人虽然没听说过，但用过后却感到困惑：“面对这张白纸，我该怎么做？功能太多太杂，具体问题解决起来却模糊不清。”（00:46:35）：但GPT的妙处在于，你可以打包呈现：“这里有个AI能完美解决的具体问题，快试试看。”用户体验后，会发现AI确实解决了问题，从而去探索其他五个场景。越来越多人将因此上线使用这些工具，因为针对特定场景的垂直工具将成为他们的破局关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in that last case, a classic horizontal product problem where it does so many things and people don't know what exactly it should do for them. So that makes a ton of sense. Just being a lot more template oriented, use case specific, helping people onboard makes tons of sense. A common problem for so many SaaS products out there. The other ones you mentioned, which was really interesting, basically more interfaces to more easily interact with OpenAI voice. You mentioned audio and things like that. That makes tons of sense. And then this agents piece where the idea is, instead of just it's a chat, it's like, "Hey, go do this thing for me." (00:47:42): Kind of along those lines, GPT-5, we touched on this a bit. There's a lot of speculation about the much better version. People just have these wild expectations, I think, for where GPT is going. GPT-5 is going to solve all the world's problems. I know you're not going to tell me when it's launching and what it's going to do, but I heard from a friend that there's kind of this tip that when you're building products today, you should build towards a GPT-5 future, not based on limitations of GPT-4 today. So to help people do that, what should people think about that might be better in a world of GPT-5? Is it just faster? It's just smarter? Is there anything else that might be like, "Oh wow, I should really rethink how I'm approaching my product?"
turns.zh:
就拿上一个案例来说，这是一个典型的横向产品问题——功能繁多却让用户不清楚它到底能为他们解决什么实际问题。因此，专注于模板导向、场景化应用、帮助用户快速上手的策略就显得尤为重要。这也是许多SaaS产品普遍面临的难题。

你提到的其他案例也很有意思，主要是为OpenAI语音接口开发更多交互界面，比如音频处理功能。这完全符合用户需求。再看智能助手模块，核心理念是从单纯的聊天功能转向主动执行任务：“嘿，帮我处理这件事吧。”（00:47:42）  

关于GPT-5，我们之前也简单提过。目前市场对其升级版充满期待，人们对GPT的未来有着不切实际的幻想，认为它能解决所有难题。虽然你不会透露具体发布时间和功能细节，但我从朋友那里听说一个建议：当下开发产品时，要着眼于GPT-5的未来潜力，而非局限于GPT-4的现有局限。那么在GPT-5时代，产品设计需要关注哪些改进点？是速度更快？智能性更强？还是有其他需要重新思考产品策略的突破点？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: If folks have looked through the GPT-4 technical report that we released back in March when GPT-4 came out, GPT-4 was the first model that we trained where we could reliably predict the capabilities of that model beforehand based on the amount of computes that we were going to put into it. We did a scientific study to show like, "Hey, this is what we predicted and here is what the actual outcome was." So it'll be, one I think, just as somebody who's interested in technology, but interesting to see does that continue to hold for GPT-5, and hopefully we'll some of that information whenever that model comes out. (00:48:56): I also think you can probably draw a few observations. One of them, which is GPT-4 came out. The consensus from the world is, "Everything is different. All of a sudden everything is different. This changes the world. This changes everything." And then slowly but surely, we come back to reality of like, "This is a really effective tool and it's going to help solve my problems more effectively." (00:49:21): And I think that is the, undoubtedly, the lens in which people should look at all of these model advancements, like GPT-5 is surely going to be extremely useful and solve some whole new echelon of problems. Hopefully it'll be faster. Hopefully It'll be better in all these ways, but fundamentally, the same problems that exists in the world are still going to be the same problems. You now just have a better tool to solve those problems. (00:49:44): And I think going back to vertical use cases, I think people who are solving very specific use cases are just now going to be able to do that much more effectively. I don't think that's going to... People have these unrealistic expectations that GPT-5 is going to be doing back flips in the background in my bedroom while it also writes all my code for me and talks on the phone with my mom or something like that. (00:50:06): I'm like, "That's not the case." It's just going to be this very effective tool, very similar to GPT-4, and it's also going to be become very normal very quickly. And I think that is actually a really interesting piece. If you can plan for the world where people become very used to these tools very quickly, I actually think that's an edge, and assuming that this thing is going to absolutely change everything, and in many ways I think it's actually a downside, is the wrong mental framing to have of these tools as they come out.
turns.zh: 假如大家看过我们在今年3月GPT-4发布时发布的技术报告，就会知道GPT-4是我们训练的首个模型，通过投入的计算量，我们能够提前可靠地预测该模型的能力。我们做了一项科学研究，证明了我们的预测结果与实际结果高度吻合。因此，作为一名科技爱好者，我很想看看这种预测能力能否在GPT-5上延续下去，希望该模型发布时能有相关信息披露。（00:48:56）：我认为大家可以从中得出一些观察结论。其中之一是GPT-4的问世。全球共识是"一切都变了，突然间一切都变了，这将改变世界，改变一切"。然而，随着时间推移，人们逐渐回归现实，意识到"这只是一款非常高效的工具，能更有效地帮助我们解决问题"。（00:49:21）：毫无疑问，人们应该以这种视角看待所有模型升级，比如GPT-5必将极其有用，能解决全新层级的问题。希望它速度更快、效果更佳，但从根本上说，世界面临的难题依然存在。现在我们只是拥有了更好的工具来解决这些问题。（00:49:44）：回到垂直应用场景，我认为那些解决特定应用的从业者将能更高效地完成任务。但我认为人们存在不切实际的期待，比如认为GPT-5能在卧室后台翻跟头、为我编写代码、和我妈妈通电话之类的。（00:50:06）：这根本不可能。它只会是一款非常高效的工具，与GPT-4非常相似，而且会迅速普及。我认为这才是真正有趣的部分。如果能让人们迅速适应这些工具，我认为这是一种优势。相反，假设GPT-5会彻底改变一切，这反而是一种错误的思维模式。

turns.zh: 是的，lennybot.com。我之前以为lennybot.com实际上是通过嵌入技术实现的。所以你把所有的知识库内容、录音、博客文章都嵌入进去。然后当人们提问时，你可以查阅问题与知识库内容的相似度，给出答案，并引用来自知识库的实证事实。这非常实用，很多人都在这么做。这就像是让这些模型扎根于现实，基于他们已知的事实。我们知道你播客中的所有内容至少是你之前说过的，在某种意义上是真实的，我们可以将这些内容引入模型根据问题生成的回答中。这真的很酷。（00:54:20）：而这些新的V3嵌入模型，再次达到最先进的性能水平，令人惊喜的是非英文语言的表现有了极大提升。过去，人们通常只将嵌入技术应用于……它在英文语境下效果显著，而现在你可以将其应用于多种新语言，因为这些语言的处理性能已大幅提升，而且成本降低了五倍，这太棒了。能为人们降低成本是最棒的感觉。我喜欢这样。我觉得现在你可以嵌入，我记得大概62,000页文本只需1美元，价格非常低廉。所以嵌入技术有很多令人兴奋的应用场景，很期待看到人们能开发出更多创新功能。

turns.zh: 是的，我觉得回归到新体验这个主题对我来说真的很兴奋。我认为消费者只会……如果你能提供聊天机器人无法获取的AI服务，你就会比其他人更具优势。人们现在大量使用聊天功能，这确实是一个非常有价值的服务领域。它之所以有价值，是因为人们在使用它。但我认为超越这种聊天界面的产品确实会占据很大优势。还有，要考虑如何将你的用例提升到下一个层次。我试用过很多非常基础的聊天示例，虽然能给我带来一点价值，但我还是会想：“这真的应该更进一步，从根本上构建你的核心体验。”（00:56:20）：我用过一款产品，它本质上能让你管理或查看网上关于特定话题的对话之类的内容。所以我可以上网看看。人们对GPT-4有什么看法？而我刚才大声说出的那句话，“人们对GPT-4有什么看法”，就是我真正想问的问题。在如今的常规产品体验中，我必须进入一堆仪表板，调整一堆过滤器之类的东西。而我真正想要的，只是提出我的问题：人们在做什么？他们对GPT-4有什么看法？然后以一种数据驱动的方式得到答案。（00:56:55）：我见过人们解决这个问题的一部分方法，比如，他们会说：“哦，好吧，这里有几个人们在说什么的例子，嗯，但这不是我真正想要的。我想要的是对正在发生的事情的总结。” 我认为只需要多花一点工程努力就能实现这一点。但我认为这就像是解锁了魔法般的体验，让人惊叹：“哇，这是一个我会继续使用的不可思议的产品，”而不是那种“嗯，这还算有点用，但我还想要更多”的感觉。

turns.zh: 我对鼓舞人心的人类故事情有独钟。最近和家人一起看的《Gran Turismo》电影，讲的是一个伦敦孩子，从虚拟赛车游戏SIM Racing起步，最终通过比赛成为职业赛车手的故事。看着他从虚拟赛车到现实赛车，再参加勒芒24小时耐力赛，这太酷了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I used to play that game and it was a lot of fun, but I don't think I have any clue how to drive a real car, race car. So that's inspiring. Do you have a favorite interview question that you'd like to ask candidates that you're interviewing?
turns.zh: 我以前也玩过那个游戏，很好玩，但我觉得我对开真车、赛车一窍不通。所以这很鼓舞人心。你有没有最喜欢的面试问题想问应聘者？

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Yeah, I'm always curious to hear what people's... The thing that they so strongly believe that people disagree with them on.
turns.zh: 有啊，我一直很好奇人们最坚信但又被他人质疑的观点是什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you look for in an answer that seems like, Wow, that's a really good signal?"
turns.zh: 你们是如何看待那种让人惊叹的回答的？比如“哇，这真是个很棒的观点！”

turns.speaker: Logan Kilpatrick
turns.en: Oftentimes, it's just an entertaining question to ask in some sense, but it's also... It's interesting to see what somebody's deeply held strong belief is, I think. And not to judge whether or not I believe in that, but just curious to see why people feel that way.
turns.zh: 很多时候，这只是一个比较有趣的问题，但也有... 我觉得看看别人的坚定信念是什么挺有意思的。我不会评判自己是否认同，但只是好奇为什么人们会有那样的看法。

turns.en: Yeah, I've got it. It's on a Post-It note that I... Right behind my camera and it's "Measure in hundreds." I love this idea of measuring things in hundreds, and it's for folks who are at the beginning of some journey. I talk to people all the time, they're like, "Yeah, I've tried this thing and it hasn't worked." And if your mental model is to measure in hundreds, "I measure in hundreds," the five times that you failed at something, you failed and tried zero times. And I love that. turns.zh: 有啊。我写在便利贴上，就在我的摄像头后面，是“用百位数衡量”。我喜欢用百位数衡量事物的这个概念，特别是对于刚开始某项旅程的人。我经常和人们聊天，比如：“是的，我试过这个方法，但没成功。” 如果你用百位数来衡量：“我用百位数衡量”，失败五次，那就是你尝试了零次。我喜欢这个概念。这很好地提醒了我们，生活中的一切都是建立在复合效应和多次尝试之上的。如果你尝试得不够多，就永远无法成功。

turns.en: I love it. What would be the joke though? We need the joke. We need the punchline. I'm just joking. I know you can't come up with amazing-

turns.zh: 我们已经被淘汰了。太棒了。洛根，非常感谢你今天的到来。最后两个问题——虽然你已经分享过这些信息了，但还是想提醒大家。如果大家想联系你或者提问，可以通过哪些渠道呢？听众又能如何为你提供帮助呢？

The model laziness was a good example where it was hard to figure out what was going on because people would be like, "Oh, the model's lazier," but it's hard to figure out what were the prompts they were using. What was the examples, all that stuff? So send those examples as you come up on things that don't work well and we'll make stuff better for you.

turns.en: Amazing. And I'll also just remind people, if you're listening to this and you're like, "Oh, okay, cool. And I know there's a lot of people just talking about this sort of thing, and I just want to remind people. Just go. Sign in. Play with it. Ask it questions on something you're working on and just see how it goes and keep coming back to it. Is there anything else you want to share along those lines to inspire people to give this a shot?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我还要提醒大家，如果你在听这期播客，然后想：“哦，嗯，酷。关于OpenAI和ChatGPT有很多很棒的想法，”你需要做的就是去chat.openai.com亲自试试。这里有很多理论探讨，但一旦你真正开始实践，就会发现视角完全不同了。目前，我每天都会在那里做些事情，比如收集问题灵感、为新闻通讯文章做研究，这个标签页我经常回访。我知道很多人都在讨论这类话题，我只想提醒大家：去试试吧。登录。用它来解决你正在处理的某个问题，观察结果如何，然后不断回访。还有其他什么想分享的吗？能激励人们尝试一下吗？

You're going to be more productive and empowered in your job and the things that you're excited about. So yeah, excited to see what people use ChatGPT for.

turns.en: And then you can expense your account. I think it's 10 or 20 bucks a month. A lot of companies are paying for this for you, so ask your boss if you can just have it expensed and make sure you use the latest version. Anyway, Logan, thank you again so much for being here.
